title: AD & DA Conversion
description: Sampling, aliasing and quantization, ADC resolution and SNR, the main ADC architectures and how a DAC builds a voltage from a code.

study.title: Sampling and aliasing
study.body: A signal with no components above $f_H$ is fully described by samples taken at $f_s > 2f_H$ (Nyquist). A component above $f_s/2$ shows up at a lower **alias** frequency: the distance to the nearest multiple $kf_s$ ($k$ = nearest integer to $f/f_s$). Aliases cannot be removed after sampling, so an analog **anti-alias low-pass filter** comes before the ADC; because real filters roll off gradually, $f_s$ is usually chosen at least 2.5–3 × $f_H$.

study.title: Quantization and resolution
study.body:
An $N$-bit ADC divides its input range $V_{FS}$ into $2^N$ zones of width $\Delta$ (1 LSB). Every voltage within one zone gets the same code, so the quantization error is up to $\Delta/2$ (rounding) or $\Delta$ (truncating). The plot shows a 3-bit, 8 V converter: 8 codes, $\Delta$ = 1 V.
To get a required resolution $\Delta_{req}$: $N \ge \log_2(V_{FS}/\Delta_{req})$, rounded **up**.

study.title: Quantization noise and SNR
study.body: The quantization error behaves like noise uniformly spread over one LSB, with rms value $\Delta/\sqrt{12}$ ($= \Delta/2\sqrt3$). For a full-scale sine wave this gives the ideal signal-to-noise ratio below: about **6 dB per bit**. A 16-bit converter gives ≈ 98 dB. A signal that uses only part of the range loses SNR: $20\log_{10}(V_p/V_{p,FS})$.

study.title: Explore: bits and quantization error
study.body: A sine wave (dashed) almost filling an 8 V range, converted with $N$ bits and played back at the middle of each code's zone. Drag $N$: every extra bit halves $\Delta$ and the staircase error, which is worth about 6 dB of SNR. With 1 or 2 bits the output is only a crude copy of the signal and the error clearly follows the signal instead of looking like noise; with 8 bits the steps are too small to see.

study.title: ADC architectures
study.body:
- **Flash**: $2^N - 1$ comparators compare the input with all levels at once. Fastest (GS/s), but large and power-hungry; usually $\le$ 8 bits.
- **Successive approximation (SAR)**: a binary search with one comparator and a DAC, one bit per clock, so $N$ clocks per conversion. The workhorse for 8–18 bits up to a few MS/s.
- **Sigma-delta (ΔΣ)**: a 1-bit converter running at a very high oversampling rate plus a digital filter; noise shaping gives 16–24 bits at low to moderate rates.
- **Dual-slope (integrating)**: slow, but averages the input and can reject mains hum; used in multimeters.

study.title: DAC and the R-2R ladder
study.body:
A DAC turns code $D$ into a voltage proportional to it. In an **R-2R ladder** each bit switches a 2R branch between ground and the virtual ground of an op amp; every section halves the current, so the bits carry binary-weighted currents $I/2, I/4, \dots$ while only two resistor values are needed. An op amp converts the summed current to a voltage.
Example: 4 bits, $V_{ref}$ = 5 V, $D = (1011)_2$ = 11: $v_o$ = 5 × 11/16 = 3.44 V.

steps.title: Sampling recap
steps.body: An ADC first **samples** the signal at rate $f_s$, then **quantizes** each sample to a code. Sampling loses nothing if $f_s > 2f_H$. A component at $f > f_s/2$ produces exactly the same samples as a lower **alias** frequency $f_a = |f - kf_s|$, with $k$ the nearest integer to $f/f_s$.

steps.prompt: A {{f|Hz}} sinusoid is sampled at {{fs|Hz}}. At what (alias) frequency do the samples appear?
steps.explanation: $f$ = {{f|Hz}} is above $f_s/2$ = {{fs/2|Hz}}, so it aliases. Nearest multiple of $f_s$: {{round(f/fs)}} × {{fs|Hz}} = {{fs*round(f/fs)|Hz}}. $f_a$ = |{{f|Hz}} − {{fs*round(f/fs)|Hz}}| = **{{abs(f-fs*round(f/fs))|Hz}}**.

steps.title: Quantization
steps.body: An $N$-bit ADC has $2^N$ codes. Its full-scale range $V_{FS}$ is split into $2^N$ steps of width $\Delta$, the **LSB** (least significant bit). That step is the resolution of the converter.

steps.prompt: Find the LSB size of a {{N}}-bit ADC with a {{VFS|V}} input range.
steps.explanation: $\Delta = V_{FS}/2^N$ = {{VFS|V}} / {{2^N||5}} = **{{VFS/2^N|V}}**. (Dividing by $2^N - 1$ is a common slip that gives a slightly different number.)

steps.prompt: How many different output codes does a 12-bit ADC have?
steps.explanation: $2^{12}$ = 4096 codes (0 to 4095). 4095 is the **largest** code, 2048 is $2^{11}$, and 12 is just the number of bits.

steps.title: Quantization noise
steps.body: The rounding error is spread evenly over ±Δ/2, so it acts like noise with rms value $\Delta/\sqrt{12}$. For a full-scale sine wave the resulting signal-to-noise ratio grows by about 6 dB for every extra bit.

steps.prompt: Find the ideal SNR of a {{N}}-bit ADC for a full-scale sinusoidal input.
steps.explanation: SNR ≈ 6.02 × {{N}} + 1.76 = **{{6.02*N+1.76|dB|4}}**. Real converters fall a few dB short; their 'effective number of bits' is lower than $N$.

steps.title: Try it: add bits
steps.body: An 8 V range, a sine input (dashed) and the quantized output. Drag the number of bits: $\Delta = V_{FS}/2^N$ halves with each bit, the error never exceeds $\Delta/2$, and its rms value $\Delta/\sqrt{12}$ sets the SNR, about 6 dB per bit.

steps.title: ADC types
steps.body:
- **Flash**: one comparator per level, all at once: fastest, but $2^N - 1$ comparators.
- **SAR**: binary search, one bit per clock cycle.
- **Sigma-delta**: heavy oversampling with a 1-bit quantizer and digital filtering: highest resolution, lower speed.
- **Dual-slope**: integrates the input: slow but rejects noise, used in multimeters.

steps.prompt: Match each ADC type to its key property
pairs: Binary search, one bit per clock
steps.explanation: Speed versus resolution: flash converters are fastest but limited to few bits; SAR converters are the general-purpose middle; sigma-delta and integrating converters trade speed for resolution and noise rejection.

steps.prompt: A flash ADC with $N$ bits needs $2^N - 1$ comparators, so going from 8 to 10 bits multiplies the number of comparators by about 4.
steps.explanation: 8 bits: 255 comparators; 10 bits: 1023. Each extra bit doubles the count, which is why flash converters rarely go beyond 8 bits, while a SAR converter needs only one comparator for any $N$.

steps.prompt: A unipolar {{N}}-bit ADC with range 0 to {{VFS|V}} **truncates**: code = $\lfloor v_{in}/\Delta \rfloor$. Which code (in decimal) does it give for $v_{in}$ = {{v||4}} V?
A {{N}}-bit DAC with reference $V_{ref}$ = {{Vr||4}} V receives code $D$ = {{D||5}} (decimal). Find its output voltage, $v_o = V_{ref}D/2^N$.
A {{N}}-bit ADC accepts inputs from −{{V|V}} to +{{V|V}}. Find the rms value of its quantization noise.
steps.explanation: The range is {{2*V|V}}, so $\Delta$ = {{2*V|V}} / {{2^N||5}} = {{2*V/2^N|V}}. $N_{q,rms} = \Delta/\sqrt{12}$ = **{{2*V/2^N/sqrt(12)|V}}**. (Using only {{V|V}} as the range is the usual mistake.)

steps.prompt: An ADC with a {{VFS|V}} input range must resolve steps of {{r|V}} or smaller. What is the minimum number of bits?
steps.explanation: Need $2^N \ge V_{FS}/\Delta_{req}$ = {{VFS|V}} / {{r|V}} = {{VFS/r||5}} levels. $\log_2$({{VFS/r||5}}) = {{ln(VFS/r)/ln(2)||4}}, rounded up: **{{ceil(ln(VFS/r)/ln(2))}} bits**.

steps.prompt: An application needs an SNR of at least {{S}} dB for a full-scale sine wave. What is the minimum number of ADC bits (ideal converter)?
The graph shows the transfer characteristic of a 3-bit ADC. Find its LSB size $\Delta$.
steps.explanation: Each step of the staircase is one LSB wide. The 8 codes cover 0 to {{VFS|V}}, so $\Delta$ = {{VFS|V}} / 8 = **{{VFS/8|V}}**. Check: $V_{FS}/2^N$ with $N$ = 3.

steps.prompt: A sinusoid of frequency $f$ is sampled at $f_s$. Which graph shows the apparent (alias) frequency of the samples as $f$ is swept from 0 to $2f_s$?
steps.explanation: Up to $f_s/2$ the samples show the true frequency. Beyond it the apparent frequency **folds back**: $f_a = |f - kf_s|$, falling to 0 at $f = f_s$, rising again to $f_s/2$ at $1.5f_s$, and so on: a triangle. It never exceeds $f_s/2$.

steps.prompt: A vibration signal of interest contains frequencies up to 5 kHz, plus noise at higher frequencies. With a good anti-alias filter in front of the ADC, which sampling rate is the sensible choice?
steps.explanation: Nyquist demands **more** than 2 × 5 kHz = 10 kHz. A real anti-alias filter cannot cut off sharply at 5 kHz, so a margin is needed: about 3 × $f_H$ = 15 kHz. 5 kHz and 8 kHz alias the signal itself; exactly 10 kHz leaves no room for the filter.

steps.prompt: An ideal {{N}}-bit ADC has range ±{{Vf|V}}, but the sine wave it digitizes has a peak of only {{Vp|V}}. Estimate the SNR.
steps.explanation: The quantization noise stays the same; the signal is {{Vp/Vf||3}} of full scale, i.e. 20 $\log_{10}$({{Vp/Vf||3}}) = {{20*log10(Vp/Vf)|dB}}. SNR ≈ 6.02 × {{N}} + 1.76 + ({{20*log10(Vp/Vf)||3}}) = **{{6.02*N+1.76+20*log10(Vp/Vf)|dB}}**. Amplify the signal to fill the range!

steps.prompt: A {{N}}-bit SAR ADC decides one bit per clock cycle of a {{fc|Hz}} clock. Ignoring any other overhead:

ask.prompt: How long does one conversion take?
ask.explanation: $N$ comparisons of one clock period each: $T = N/f_{clk}$ = {{N}} / {{fc|Hz}} = **{{N/fc|s}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the maximum sampling rate (samples per second)?
ask.explanation: One conversion takes $N/f_{clk}$, so at most $f_{clk}/N$ = {{fc|Hz}} / {{N}} = **{{fc/N|S/s}}** conversions per second.

steps.prompt: A 4-bit SAR ADC with $V_{ref}$ = 16 V (so 1 LSB = 1 V) converts $v_{in}$ = {{v||3}} V. It first tries 1000 (8 V). What DAC voltage does it try in its **third** comparison?
steps.explanation: 1st trial: {{v||3}} V compared with 8 V $\to$ MSB = {{b3}}. 2nd trial: {{8*b3}} + 4 = {{8*b3+4}} V $\to$ next bit = {{b2}}. 3rd trial: {{8*b3}} + {{4*b2}} + 2 = **{{8*b3+4*b2+2}} V**. A bit is kept when $v_{in}$ is at least the trial voltage.

steps.prompt: Oversampling by a factor $M$ (then averaging/filtering down to the original rate) improves the SNR by $10\log_{10}M$ dB if the quantization noise is white. By what factor must you oversample to gain {{k}} extra bit(s) of resolution?
steps.explanation: One bit is 6.02 dB, so you need {{6.02*k||3}} dB: $10\log_{10}M$ = {{6.02*k||3}} $\to$ $M$ = 10^({{0.602*k||3}}) ≈ **{{4^k}}**, i.e. $4^k$. Plain oversampling is expensive; sigma-delta converters add noise shaping to do much better.

steps.prompt: A 4-bit R-2R DAC with $V_{ref}$ = {{Vr|V}} receives the binary code {{mod(floor(D/8),2)}}{{mod(floor(D/4),2)}}{{mod(floor(D/2),2)}}{{mod(floor(D/1),2)}}. Find the output voltage magnitude $V_{ref}D/2^N$.
steps.explanation: Binary {{mod(floor(D/8),2)}}{{mod(floor(D/4),2)}}{{mod(floor(D/2),2)}}{{mod(floor(D/1),2)}} in decimal: $D$ = 8·{{mod(floor(D/8),2)}} + 4·{{mod(floor(D/4),2)}} + 2·{{mod(floor(D/2),2)}} + {{mod(D,2)}} = {{D}}. Each bit contributes a binary-weighted share ($V_{ref}/2$, $/4$, $/8$, $/16$). $v_o$ = {{Vr|V}} × {{D}} / 16 = **{{Vr*D/16|V}}**.

steps.prompt: A sensor gives at most ±{{Vp|V}}. It is amplified to fill an ADC range of ±5 V, and the system must resolve {{r|V}} at the **sensor**.

ask.explanation: Gain = 5 V / {{Vp|V}} = **{{5/Vp||4}}**, so the sensor's full range maps onto the ADC's full range.

ask.prompt: What is the minimum number of ADC bits?
ask.explanation: The sensor span {{2*Vp|V}} must be split into steps of {{r|V}}: {{2*Vp/r||5}} levels. $\log_2$({{2*Vp/r||5}}) = {{ln(2*Vp/r)/ln(2)||4}} $\to$ **{{ceil(ln(2*Vp/r)/ln(2))}} bits** (choose the next standard size for margin). The gain does not change this: it scales signal and LSB alike.

steps.prompt: A sigma-delta ADC uses a very coarse (often 1-bit) quantizer at a high oversampling rate, and gets its high resolution from noise shaping and digital filtering.
steps.explanation: The modulator pushes quantization noise to high frequencies (noise shaping); the digital decimation filter removes it and lowers the rate. That is how 1-bit hardware achieves 16–24-bit resolution at audio and measurement rates.
